transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-21 15:00 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Elliot Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (StratoGrid), Nadia Ruiz (StratoGrid), Marcus Lee (StratoGrid)

Summary:
Quick integration discovery focused on how StratoGrid would plug Redwood into their existing inference gateway and orchestration. Main concerns: minimal code changes for SDKs, how to route traffic through an internal proxy, throttling and quota enforcement, and visibility into per-request token costs and traces. Agreed to pilot a gateway-forwarding POC and a security deep dive.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run about 45 minutes, just to get a sense of StratoGrid's current stack and where Redwood could fit. Uh, quick intros?
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Yeah, hi, Liam here, head of platform at StratoGrid. We run a Kubernetes heavy infra, have an internal API gateway that mediates all model calls and does auth. Nadia's our ML infra lead, Marcus is on security.
[00:22] Nadia Ruiz: Hi all, thanks. We are evaluating options between running dedicated infra versus using a hosted provider; primary constraints are PII data flow and SSO/KMS integration.
[00:32] Elliot Ramos: Awesome. Quick note — Redwood supports hosted, dedicated and private VPC. For integration, the typical patterns are: direct SDK calls from service, routed via a company gateway/proxy, or via a sidecar that handles batching and KV cache. Which of these maps to how you currently talk to models?
[00:48] Marcus Lee: We currently proxy everything through our gateway, yes. We also have rate limit rules on the gateway and some request enrichment headers for tracing.
[00:58] Priya Singh: When you say rate limit, are those per-user or per-service? Just to understand quotas.
[01:03] Marcus Lee: Per-service mostly, plus some per-customer soft limits. We need to ensure Redwood doesn't override our upstream throttling and that we can enforce spikes.
[01:12] Maya Chen: Totally. Redwood has quota controls on the account and token side, and you can set per-route quotas if you run Dedicated or Private. For hosted, we expose API keys and rate limiting at the API key level — and there's an enterprise routing feature for sticky capacity.
[01:27] Liam O'Connor: Ok, our engineering team is using LangChain in python and a small set of microservices using Node for orchestration. Any prebuilt adapters?
[01:36] Elliot Ramos: Yes — we have SDKs in Python and Node, and we maintain LangChain and LlamaIndex examples. There's a sample adapter for LangChain chains that uses Redwood streaming and function-calling. I'll send the repo link after. The adapter handles retries and backpressure so you can plug it in with minimal changes.
[01:52] Nadia Ruiz: Are those adapters opinionated about batching or do we control batching behavior? We run a lot of small prompts; batching could help cost but may increase latency.
[02:03] Elliot Ramos: Good question. Batching is configurable. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching with batching windows and max batch size. You can also opt-out per-route or per-call. For low-latency calls, you'd set small batch windows or disable batching.
[02:18] Liam O'Connor: From a gateway perspective, we want the gateway to be able to do header-based routing to different models based on customer tier. Can Redwood accept annotated headers for model selection?
[02:27] Maya Chen: Yep, you can pass model hints via headers or params — on Dedicated/Private you can policy-route at the edge. For hosted we support a routing policy that you can configure from the Console — e.g., route enterprise keys to smaller latency specialized pools.
[02:43] Marcus Lee: About observability: we need per-request tracing, token counts, and cost. How do we get spans into our existing tracing system (Jaeger/Datadog)?
[02:52] Priya Singh: We surface per-request breadcrumbs in our response metadata and also have tracing hooks — you can push traces via OpenTelemetry or instrument the SDK to emit spans. There's also a webhook for delivery of usage events if you want to ingest into your pipeline.
[03:08] Nadia Ruiz: The webhook option — is that high-volume friendly? We have spikes to 1k QPS at peak.
[03:13] Elliot Ramos: Webhooks are intended for async events and you'd want to use our streaming metrics API or direct Prometheus scrape endpoints for high-volume telemetry. For Dedicated we support Prometheus exporters inside the cluster.
[03:26] Liam O'Connor: How would a typical proxy setup look? We want minimal code in the gateway; ideally the gateway just proxies to Redwood with auth headers.
[03:34] Maya Chen: Typical patterns: 1) Gateway forwards request to Redwood hosted API using API key — simple. 2) Gateway forwards to a Redwood-managed private endpoint in your VPC — better for data residency. 3) Gateway forwards to Dedicated endpoints inside your network if you've reserved capacity. If you want enrichment, you can include your trace IDs in headers and Redwood will echo them in logs.
[03:55] Marcus Lee: KMS — we need keys to be customer-managed. Is KMS supported for Private?
[03:59] Maya Chen: Yes, Private supports customer KMS and HSM integrations. For Hosted we offer encryption at rest and managed keys, and enterprise customers can bring keys with some constraints — we'll share the KMS matrix.
[04:12] Liam O'Connor: On pricing and quotas: what's the simplest way to enforce per-tenant spend limits?
[04:18] Priya Singh: You can create API keys per-tenant and attach quota policies, soft and hard limits, and thresholds. Redwood Console will surface alerts when usage approaches quotas, and you can wire webhooks for cutover. For Dedicated, you can map tenants to routes that consume from specific GPU pools to isolate spend.
[04:33] Nadia Ruiz: About SDK behavior — is the Node SDK able to stream tokens back incrementally for server-sent events? We rely on streaming in some real-time features.
[04:41] Elliot Ramos: Yes, streaming supported in both Python and Node. We provide SSE and websocket-based streaming modes; the SDK wraps the complexity. Note that network middleboxes sometimes buffer streams — so streaming through gateway needs to preserve transfer-encoding.
[04:59] Liam O'Connor: Hmm, we have a layer of Envoy that sometimes transforms chunked encoding. Any tips?
[05:05] Elliot Ramos: We generally recommend passthrough config for streaming endpoints or using a sidecar that terminates streaming and forwards aggregated deltas. We can share an Envoy sample config.
[05:16] Marcus Lee: From a security posture, we'll need SOC2 type II, audit logs, SSO — do you support SAML/SCIM?
[05:25] Maya Chen: Yes, SAML and SCIM for user provisioning; audit logs are available in Console and we can stream logs to your SIEM. Dedicated/Private gives you longer retention windows and the option to keep logs in your cloud account.
[05:38] Nadia Ruiz: For the pilot, we want to run a small test that exercises gateway-forwarding, streaming, and a LangChain chain. Can Redwood capture per-prompt pass/fail for our quality checks?
[05:48] Priya Singh: We have structured outputs and eval hooks — you can attach a prompt id and Redwood will associate tokens, latencies, and model outputs to that id for later quality regression detection. We'll walk through an example in the sample repo.
[06:02] Liam O'Connor: Great. Regarding model variants: how do rollouts work? We sometimes want A/B between older and newer model checkpoint to check hallucination rates.
[06:09] Elliot Ramos: Rollouts are supported with canaries and percentage traffic splits per route. Console will show metrics and quality regressions can trigger automatic rollback if you choose that policy.
[06:20] Marcus Lee: A note on data retention — for compliance we need to ensure certain sessions are never stored. Is that doable?
[06:27] Maya Chen: Yes, you can set no-retention flags on calls. For Hosted, by default we don't persist customer data for training, and we can turn off logging for specific keys. For Private, you control storage. We'll share the data retention policy doc.
[06:40] Nadia Ruiz: One practical question: how long is an SDK upgrade path? We have older in-house wrappers and will need to migrate incrementally.
[06:48] Elliot Ramos: Our SDKs are backwards-compatible for the most part; we have a small shim for old v1 calls. The LangChain adapter also supports an adapter layer so you can point to Redwood with minimal change.
[06:59] Liam O'Connor: For the pilot perf targets, we want 95th latency under 250ms for short prompts and throughput of ~200 rps for our test set. Is that reasonable?
[07:10] Priya Singh: Short prompts with smaller models should be achievable on Dedicated with tuned batching and fixed token budgets. For Hosted, tail latency depends on pool and concurrency; we'll propose a configuration. We'll include quantization suggestions if you accept slightly lower quality to hit cost/latency goals.
[07:27] Marcus Lee: Are there any constraints when running through our gateway in terms of auth rotation? We rotate keys every 24 hours.
[07:33] Maya Chen: API keys can be rotated; we support short-lived tokens and mutual TLS for Dedicated/Private endpoints. We can also integrate with your identity provider for session tokens.
[07:44] Liam O'Connor: Ok, on observability — can we get Prometheus metrics per-model and per-route?
[07:49] Elliot Ramos: Yes, Prometheus exporter exposes per-model, per-route token counts, latency histograms, batch sizes. For hosted customers we surface aggregated metrics; for Dedicated/Private you get finer-grained scraping.
[08:04] Nadia Ruiz: For the webhook of events — can we get the raw token usage per call? We want to reconcile billable tokens to our internal metering.
[08:11] Priya Singh: We can provide usage events including token breakdown per call, model used, and request id. For high RPS we'd recommend using bulk export endpoints or streaming metrics to avoid webhook saturation.
[08:25] Liam O'Connor: Good. Any limitations on LLama-family models or specific quantized runtimes? We do use some custom quantized checkpoints in-house.
[08:33] Elliot Ramos: Redwood supports a wide catalog, and for Dedicated/Private you can bring custom models — there are packaging and compatibility checks. Quantization is supported but some extreme quant formats require a tune. We'll coordinate model onboarding.
[08:48] Marcus Lee: Regarding logs and audit — can customers retain raw request/response payloads in their own S3?
[08:55] Maya Chen: For Dedicated/Private yes. For hosted, we can push events to your cloud bucket with proper agreements and options; otherwise we manage storage and give you access to exports.
[09:07] Nadia Ruiz: Ok, let's talk about a minimal POC plan. What would Redwood need from us to start?
[09:13] Elliot Ramos: Ideally: 1) sample traffic profile (QPS, prompt size distribution), 2) a sandbox API key or route to test through your gateway, 3) a small LangChain example to run against Redwood. We'll set up monitoring and a dashboard for the pilot.
[09:27] Liam O'Connor: We can provide traffic snapshots and a small test harness. Timeline — we want to start the pilot in two weeks.
[09:33] Maya Chen: Sounds doable. We'll send the onboarding checklist and a proposed pilot configuration.
[09:39] Marcus Lee: Final question — do you have a hard SLA for tail latency on Dedicated?
[09:44] Priya Singh: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLO-backed latency targets depending on the GPU profile and model family; exact SLA terms are in the Dedicated contract. We'll attach an example SLA in the follow-ups.
[09:56] Maya Chen: Ok let's recap next steps...
[10:00] [10:00-47:00] -- (discussion continues with deeper technical Q&A, Elliot shares specific Envoy config, Maya confirms pricing band and next call scheduling) --

Wrap-up recap (from Maya):
- Redwood to send LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter repo, Envoy sample config, pilot checklist, and pricing for Dedicated options.
- StratoGrid to provide traffic profile, list of endpoints that will proxy to Redwood, and security requirements for KMS/SAML.
- Schedule security deep dive with Marcus, target week of 10/27.
